title: Cap. IX Arg. 7 Sol close: theft/homicide do not precede hanging as means procured by the judge — so reprobates' sins precede damnation as presupposed matter (Cajetan)
latin: Sicut igitur furtum aut homicidium non praecedit suspendium furis aut homicidae tanquam medium a judice in eum finem procuratum et adhibitum, sed tantum ut quiddam praesuppositum, sic peccata reprobatorum praecedunt eorum damnationem. Potest igitur Deus justissime damnare omnes infideles et impoenitentes, quia licet infidelitas sequatur reprobationem, tamen est extra totum reprobationis effectum, et nascitur ex corde reprobati; non eam operante, efficiente, aut proliciente Deo, sed praevidente, permittente, et per gratiam specialis misericordiae non impediente, quia non tenetur eum in modum impedire. Vide Cajetanum, in 1. quaest. 23. art. 5.
pass_a: As therefore theft or homicide does not precede the hanging of the thief or homicide as a means procured and applied by the judge unto that end, but only as something presupposed, so the sins of the reprobate precede their damnation. God can therefore most justly damn all the unbelieving and impenitent, because although unbelief follows reprobation, yet it is outside the whole effect of reprobation, and is born from the heart of the reprobate; God not working, effecting, or drawing it forth, but foreseeing, permitting, and by the grace of special mercy not impeding it, because he is not bound so to impede it. See Cajetan, in 1. quaest. 23. art. 5.
pass_b: Just as theft or homicide does not precede the hanging of thief or murderer as a means the judge procured and applied for that end — only as something presupposed — so the reprobates' sins precede their damnation. God can therefore most justly damn all unbelievers and impenitents: though unbelief follows reprobation, it lies outside the whole effect of reprobation and is born from the reprobate's heart. God does not work, effect, or draw it forth; he foresees, permits, and by special-mercy grace does not impede it — for he is not bound so to impede it. See Cajetan on ST 1 q.23 a.5.

lemmas.gloss: crime presupposed for hanging, not judge-procured means

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8: absolute reprobation not from foresight of actual sins makes God deal more rigidly with some men than with the very devils
latin: Qui statuunt Deum mera sua voluntate, et non ex praevisione actualium peccatorum et finalis perseverantiae in iisdem, quosdam reprobasse, illi statuunt Deum longe rigidius agere cum hominibus quibusdam, quam cum ipsis diabolis: Cum enim diaboli excludantur a vita ob peccata quae propria sua malitia commiserunt, homines quidam reprobati ponuntur, non propter propria peccata quae in personis suis commiserunt, sed tantum considerati uti alieno peccato Adami ex imputatione Divina rei.
pass_a: They who establish that God by his mere will, and not from foresight of actual sins and of final perseverance in the same, has reprobated certain ones, those establish that God deals far more rigidly with certain men than with the very devils: For whereas the devils are excluded from life on account of sins which by their own proper malice they committed, certain reprobated men are placed not on account of proper sins which in their persons they committed, but only considered as guilty by Divine imputation of the alien sin of Adam.
pass_b: Those who hold that God by mere will — not from foresight of actual sins and final perseverance in them — has reprobated some, thereby hold that God deals far more rigidly with certain men than with the very devils. For the devils are shut out of life for sins they committed by their own malice; yet some reprobated men are set not for sins done in their own persons, but only as guilty by divine imputation of Adam's alien sin.

lemmas.gloss: adversaries: absolute reprobation harder on men than on demons
men reprobated as guilty only by Adam's imputed sin

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8: Borrius and Arminius — no one damned for original sin alone; Remonstrants at Dort: infants incapable of disobedience not punished with eternal pain
latin: Borrius quidam hoc argumento probare conatus est, ob peccatum originale neminem condemnari, atque idcirco omnes omnium gentilium infantes morientes ante commissionem actualium peccatorum salvos esse: ut videre licet apud Arminium, in Respons. ad art. 13. et 14. In hac autem sententia fuisse constitutum ipsum Arminium, et Arminianos eandem nunc defendere clarum est. Corvinus, qui fuit Arminio ab intimis consiliis, sic scribit, pag. 391. Equidem Arminius statuit, neminem propter solum peccatum originis damnari. Atque Remonstrantes citati ad Synodum Dordracenam, in scripto publice et communi omnium eorum consensu exhibito, aperte dixerunt: Nullos infantes, utpote qui novae inobedientiae et rebellionis capaces non sunt, poena aeterna puniri.
pass_a: A certain Borrius tried by this argument to prove that on account of original sin no one is condemned, and therefore that all infants of all the Gentiles dying before the commission of actual sins are saved: as may be seen in Arminius, in Respons. ad art. 13. and 14. But that Arminius himself was established in this sentence, and that the Arminians now defend the same, is clear. Corvinus, who was of Arminius's inward counsels, so writes, pag. 391. Indeed Arminius establishes that no one is damned on account of original sin alone. And the Remonstrants cited unto the Synod of Dort, in a writing publicly and by the common consent of them all exhibited, openly said: That no infants, inasmuch as they are not capable of new disobedience and rebellion, are punished with eternal pain.
pass_b: A certain Borrius tried by this argument to prove that no one is condemned for original sin, and so that all Gentile infants dying before actual sins are saved — as may be seen in Arminius, Respons. to arts. 13–14. That Arminius himself held this, and that Arminians still defend it, is clear. Corvinus, of Arminius's inner counsel, writes (p. 391): Indeed Arminius holds that no one is damned for original sin alone. And the Remonstrants cited to the Synod of Dort, in a writing shown publicly by common consent of them all, said openly: No infants — inasmuch as they are not capable of new disobedience and rebellion — are punished with eternal pain.

lemmas.gloss: no damnation for original sin alone
Dort Remonstrants: infants not eternally punished

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8 Sol first: from Arminian concessions — if all are made guilty of eternal death by Adam's imputed act alone, God deals more rigidly with men than with demons
latin: Respondeo primo, Posse nos ex concessis Arminianorum non dissimile argumentum texere, quod tamen nullius momenti esse ipsi proculdubio affirmabunt. Nam illud notandum est: Quamvis constanter negent ob innatum peccatum originale damnari quenquam, tamen e contrario coguntur illorum capita, agnoscunt mortis reatum etiam in parvulos omnes esse derivatum ex imputatione actualis ejus peccati quod ab Adamo admissum fuit. Hoc itaque solummodo concesso sic licet nobis argumentari: Qui statuunt Deum omnes homines, tam infantes quam adultos, aeternae mortis reos in strictum jus conferre, ex eo solum quod imputatur illis peccatum quod non actuale in propria uniuscujusque persona commissum, sed ab Adamo perpetratum, illi faciunt Deum rigidius agentem cum hominibus quam cum diabolis: Nam nemo diabolorum reus censetur nisi ob peccatum in propria persona, et ex propria malitia commissum; at homines, ex sententia Arminii, rei mortis aeternae constituuntur, tantum considerati uti alieni peccati Adami ex imputatione Divina rei. Quicquid responsi nobis dederint, idem nos et illis regeremus.
pass_a: I answer first, That we can from the concessions of the Arminians weave a not unlike argument, which yet they themselves will doubtless affirm to be of no moment. For this is to be noted: Although they constantly deny that anyone is damned on account of innate original sin, yet on the contrary their heads are compelled, they acknowledge that the guilt of death even unto all little ones has been derived from the imputation of that actual sin which was committed by Adam. This therefore only being granted, so it is lawful for us to argue: They who establish that God confers all men, infants as well as adults, as guilty of eternal death into strict right, from this alone that there is imputed unto them a sin which is not actual committed in each one's proper person, but perpetrated by Adam, those make God dealing more rigidly with men than with the demons: For no one of the demons is counted guilty except on account of sin committed in his proper person, and from his proper malice; but men, on Arminius's sentence, are constituted guilty of eternal death, only considered as guilty by Divine imputation of Adam's alien sin. Whatever answer they shall have given us, the same we would also retort upon them.
pass_b: First I answer: from Arminian concessions we can weave a like argument, which they themselves will doubtless call of no moment. Note this: though they constantly deny anyone is damned for innate original sin, they are forced the other way — they grant that guilt of death has been derived even to all infants from imputation of that actual sin Adam committed. Grant only that, and we may argue: those who hold God puts all men, infants and adults, under strict right as guilty of eternal death merely because a sin not done in each one's own person but by Adam is imputed to them, make God deal more rigidly with men than with demons. No demon is counted guilty except for sin done in his own person from his own malice; yet on Arminius's view men are made guilty of eternal death only as guilty by divine imputation of Adam's alien sin. Whatever reply they give us, we will turn the same back on them.

lemmas.gloss: retort from their own concessions on Adam's imputation
demons guilty only for own-person sins

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8 Sol second: comparing rigor in reprobating men vs demons is inept — reprobation is denial of an undue benefit, not an act decreeing punishment
latin: Verum quia, ut vulgo dici solet, contra agere non est solvere, respondemus secundo: Quando quaeritur utrum major justitiae rigor exerceatur in reprobatione hominum an Daemonum, ineptam prorsus esse comparationem, si constet rigidam justitiam neutris reprobandis exerceri. Cum igitur reprobatio sit indebiti beneficii negatio (puta infallibilis ordinationis ad vitam aeternam per specialis gratiae praeparationem et donationem) profecto nec hominum nec angelorum reprobatio fuit actus rigidae justitiae, imo ne justitiae quidem proprie et formaliter dictae; quamvis non fuerit contra justitiam, sicut nec ullus actus Divinus, et eo sensu justissima appelletur. Inepte igitur in reprobatione rigidae justitiae gradus ponderant, cum mera reprobatio, sive hominum sive daemonum, non sit actus poenam decernentis, in quo rigor possit considerari, sed actus beneficium negantis, in quo sola Dei libertas debet attendi.
pass_a: But because, as is commonly said, to act against is not to solve, we answer secondly: When it is asked whether greater rigor of justice is exercised in the reprobation of men or of Demons, the comparison is utterly inept, if it be established that rigid justice is exercised in reprobating neither. Since therefore reprobation is the denial of an undue benefit (namely of an infallible ordination unto eternal life through the preparation and gift of special grace) assuredly neither the reprobation of men nor of angels was an act of rigid justice, nay not even of justice properly and formally so called; although it was not against justice, as neither is any Divine act, and in that sense may be called most just. Ineptly therefore in reprobation they weigh degrees of rigid justice, since mere reprobation, whether of men or of demons, is not an act of one decreeing punishment, in which rigor can be considered, but an act of one denying a benefit, in which the sole liberty of God ought to be attended unto.
pass_b: But as the saying goes, to counter-argue is not to solve — so second: when the question is whether greater rigor of justice is used in reprobating men or demons, the comparison is wholly inept if rigid justice is exercised in reprobating neither. Reprobation is denial of an undue benefit — namely of infallible ordination to eternal life through preparation and gift of special grace. So neither men's nor angels' reprobation was an act of rigid justice — not even of justice properly and formally so called — though it was not against justice (as no divine act is), and in that sense may be called most just. Inept, then, to weigh degrees of rigid justice in reprobation: mere reprobation, of men or demons, is not an act decreeing punishment (where rigor could be considered) but an act denying a benefit, where only God's liberty is to be regarded.

lemmas.gloss: reprobation = denial of undue benefit, not punitive rigor
attend liberty of God, not degrees of rigid justice

title: Cap. IX Arg. 8 Sol third: foundation rotten — blessed angels elected, damned angels passed over, not from foresight of merits/rebellion but from mere liberty of will
latin: Tertio, ipsum fundamentum cui innititur tota haec argumentatio putridum est: Nam videtur pro concesso sumere, Diabolos fuisse ex praevisione actualium suorum peccatorum reprobatos. At nos e contra dicimus, Angelos beatos ante jacta mundi fundamenta fuisse electos, non ex praevisis eorundem meritis, sed ex pura gratia eligentis; et Angelos damnatos fuisse pariter ab aeterno praeteritos, non-electos, sive reprobatos, non ex praevisione futurae rebellionis et finalis in eadem obdurationis, sed ex mera voluntate sive libertate Dei hanc gratiam illis donare nolentis. Si igitur Arminiani a Diabolorum reprobatione probare volunt homines minime fuisse reprobatos, nisi ex antecedente praevisione et consideratione actualium peccatorum, debuerunt hoc prius solido argumento aliquo confirmare quoad reprobationem daemonum, quam inde de hominum reprobatione consequentias inferre.
pass_a: Thirdly, the very foundation upon which this whole argumentation leans is rotten: For it seems to take as granted that the Devils were reprobated from foresight of their actual sins. But we on the contrary say that the blessed Angels before the foundations of the world were laid were elected, not from their foresighted merits, but from the pure grace of the electing One; and that the damned Angels were likewise from eternity passed by, non-elect, or reprobated, not from foresight of future rebellion and of final hardening in the same, but from the mere will or liberty of God not willing to give them this grace. If therefore the Arminians from the reprobation of the Devils wish to prove that men were by no means reprobated except from antecedent foresight and consideration of actual sins, they ought first to have confirmed this by some solid argument as to the reprobation of the demons, before inferring thence consequences concerning the reprobation of men.
pass_b: Third: the very foundation this whole argument leans on is rotten. It seems to take as granted that the Devils were reprobated from foresight of their actual sins. We say the contrary: the blessed angels were elected before the world's foundations were laid — not from foresighted merits but from the electing One's pure grace; and the damned angels were likewise from eternity passed by, non-elect, or reprobated — not from foresight of future rebellion and final hardening in it, but from God's mere will or liberty not willing to give them that grace. So if Arminians from the Devils' reprobation want to prove men were reprobated only from antecedent foresight of actual sins, they ought first to confirm that by solid argument for the demons' reprobation before drawing consequences about men's.

lemmas.gloss: blessed angels elected from pure grace, not foresight merits
damned angels passed over from mere liberty, not foresight rebellion
